title: Don't Confuse Role Design With Job Design
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that a common and consequential leadership error is collapsing two distinct design problems — job design and role design — into one, which produces weak candidate assessment and poor hires. Job design answers 'what tasks does this person perform,' while role design answers the broader question of 'what contribution is this person expected to make,' including the authority, decision rights, and collaboration needed to make that contribution. The essay prescribes a specific sequence for leaders creating or filling a position: design the role first (the contribution and its fit in the organization), then design the job (the specific tasks), and only then define success criteria that draw on both. Its closing argument is that the two are complementary rather than competing, and that skipping either produces a predictable failure mode — a job without role clarity invites busywork without direction, while a role without task specificity gives no clear path to executing it well.
points: Job design answers 'what tasks does this person perform,' while role design answers the broader question of 'what contribution is this person expected to make,' including authority, decision rights, and required collaboration.
The recommended sequence is role design first (contribution and organizational fit), job design second (specific tasks), and success criteria last, defined from both together.
A job without role clarity is said to invite busywork without direction, while a role without task specificity provides no clear path to executing it well.
The piece frames blurring the two together as a direct cause of weak candidate assessment and poor hiring selection.
quotes: Leaders who create positions based on outcomes often forget to specify the fixed list of tasks and skills required, while those who focus on tasks and capabilities often neglect the larger purpose the role must serve.
Job design is about the tasks and activities that make up a team position. The design asks and answers the question, "What tasks does this person perform?
In contrast, role design is about broader purpose, responsibilities, and relationships. A well-designed role focuses on the question, "What contribution is this person expected to make?

Best practice suggests that leaders first design the role by specifying the desired contribution and how it will fit into the organization. Next, they should design the job by defining the tasks the person will perform.
A job without role clarity invites busywork without direction, and a role without task specificity provides no clear path to excellent execution.
